title: How Giraffes Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain giraffes, prompted by a request from six-year-old Mika after a Vancouver live show. They cover the history of the "camel leopard" name and Darwin's neck theory, giraffe taxonomy (Giraffa camelopardalis, okapi as close relative, the 2016 four-species study and its caveats), the giraffe's tall anatomy (vertebrae, recurrent laryngeal nerve, heart pressure, compression-sock hide), tongue, eyes and senses, coat patterns and camouflage, the white giraffes in Kenya, habitat, predators and running, social "towers," sleep, vocalizations, oxpecker symbiosis, male necking and ossicones, calving and calf survival, grief in mothers, diet and rumination, ecological role, conservation decline, and World Giraffe Day. The episode closes with listener mail thanks.

segments.title: Opening and Mika's request
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode as a special Animal Edition requested by six-year-old Mika at a Vancouver live show, and joke about children and giraffes.

segments.title: Camel leopards and Darwin's neck theory
segments.summary: The hosts describe the old name 'camel leopard' and the scientific name Giraffa camelopardalis. They discuss Darwin's drought-and-famine idea for the giraffe's neck, the criticism that giraffes still feed at the same level as other animals, and Lamarck's stretching-antelope idea.

segments.title: Classification and species debate
segments.summary: The hosts cover the giraffe's classification as an even-toed ungulate, the giraffid family with the giraffe and okapi genera, and the okapi's split about eleven million years ago. They discuss the 2016 study proposing four giraffe species and note that the classification is not yet settled.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the anatomy discussion.

segments.title: Giraffe height, neck vertebrae and nerves
segments.summary: The hosts explain that giraffes have the same seven cervical vertebrae as other mammals, each about eleven inches long, and six-foot legs. They cover the fifteen-foot recurrent laryngeal nerve as an example of an evolutionary workaround, plus the sizes of males and females.

segments.title: Tongue, heart and circulation adaptations
segments.summary: The hosts describe the giraffe's long prehensile tongue, large feet, and a heart about two feet long and around twenty-five pounds with thick walls that pump at high pressure. They explain that the tight hide acts like a compression sock to keep blood from pooling in the legs.

segments.title: Coat patterns, camouflage and habitat
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how each giraffe's coat pattern is unique, varying by region (Masai, Uganda, reticulated), and how camouflage helps them hide among trees. They mention the all-white giraffes in Kenya, which are not albino but have lucism, and describe their savanna habitat.

segments.title: Vision, predators and running
segments.summary: The hosts describe giraffes' large eyes, peripheral vision and color vision, their vulnerability to lions and other predators, and their ability to run fast in short bursts. They discuss the graceful gallop-like running they have seen at zoos.

segments.title: Towers, sleep, voice and oxpeckers
segments.summary: The hosts explain that a group of giraffes is called a tower, with loose and mixed membership and no territories. They cover short sleep periods, quiet vocalizations and possible low-frequency humming, snorting as an alarm, and the oxpecker relationship that warns giraffes of lions.

segments.title: Necking, ossicones and calving
segments.summary: The hosts describe male combat over access to females, the ossicones and calcium deposits, young males imitating adults, and the fourteen-month gestation and dramatic birth. They also note how quickly calves stand and walk.

segments.title: Calf survival, maternal behavior and grief
segments.summary: The hosts explain that only about one in four infant giraffes survive the first year. They describe how mothers leave calves hidden for long periods, and a documented case of a mother grieving a lost calf for four days.

segments.title: Diet, rumination and water
segments.summary: The hosts cover the giraffe's herbivorous diet of acacia and mimosa leaves, its prehensile lips and tongue for avoiding thorns, the amount of foliage eaten, and rumination with four stomach chambers. They also mention that giraffes can go weeks without drinking water.

segments.title: Ecological role and conservation
segments.summary: The hosts describe giraffes' role in pruning trees and spreading seeds. They discuss population decline from about 140,000 to about 80,000 over fifteen years, mostly from poaching and habitat loss, plus the use of giraffe tails, and the designation of World Giraffe Day on June 21.

segments.title: Listener mail and thanks
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners for gifts including whiskey, ketchup, skincare products, socks, books, and a graphic novel, and mention a part two of listener mail is planned.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck list ways to contact the show and sign off.
